record.paper_title: Recent progress and open questions on the numerical index of Banach spaces
record.original_question: Determine whether the numerical index of ℓ_p equals the numerical index of its two-dimensional version ℓ_p^2 for every 1 < p < ∞; that is, whether n(ℓ_p) = n(ℓ_p^2).

evidence.quote: Problem 4. Is it true that n(ℓp) = n(ℓ2p) for every 1 < p < ∞?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $1<p<\infty$. For a real Banach space $X$, denote by $B_X$ its closed unit ball and by $S_X$ its unit sphere. For a bounded linear operator $T\colon X\to X$, define its numerical radius by
$$v(T)=\sup\{\,|x^{*}(T x)| : x\in S_X,\ x^{*}\in S_{X^{*}},\ x^{*}(x)=1\,\},$$
and define the numerical index of $X$ by
$$n(X)=\inf\{\,v(T) : T\in\mathcal{L}(X),\ \|T\|=1\,\}.$$
Let $\ell_p$ denote the real Banach space of $p$-summable sequences with its standard norm, and let $\ell_p^{2}$ denote the two-dimensional real space $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ equipped with the norm $\|(x_1,x_2)\|_p=(|x_1|^p+|x_2|^p)^{1/p}$.

Determine whether
$$n(\ell_p)=n(\ell_p^{2})$$
holds for every $1<p<\infty$.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is part of a well-known set of problems about numerical indices of $\ell_p$ spaces. It is known that $n(\ell_p) = \inf_{m\in\mathbb{N}} n(\ell_p^{m})$, and explicit formulas for $n(\ell_p^{2})$ have been computed in certain ranges of $p$, but no published result establishes the equality $n(\ell_p)=n(\ell_p^{2})$ for all $1<p<\infty$. The problem appears to still be open.

status_evidence.title: On the numerical index of real L_p(μ)-spaces
status_evidence.snippet: n(L_p(μ)) = n(ℓ_p) = inf_{m∈ℕ} n(ℓ_p^m); numerical index of ℓ_p^2 computed in specific ranges of p.
status_evidence.claim: It is known that n(ℓ_p) equals the infimum of n(ℓ_p^m) over m, but the question of whether this infimum is attained at m=2 remains unresolved.

status_evidence.title: The numerical index of ℓp2
status_evidence.snippet: Computation/estimation of the numerical index of the two-dimensional space ℓ_p^2.
status_evidence.claim: Recent work continues to study n(ℓ_p^2), indicating the comparison with n(ℓ_p) is not fully resolved.
